key_terms.meaning: Welding in which the parent metal melts at the joint, with or without a filler; coalescence occurs in the liquid state.
Welding in which the parent metal stays solid and coalescence comes from pressure, heat and diffusion at clean contacting surfaces.
Joining with a filler that melts above 450 °C but below the parent metal; the liquid filler flows by capillary action and the parent does not melt.
A fusion weld made without added filler metal; the parent metal alone forms the joint.
The joining of two surfaces into one continuous body by atomic or molecular attraction.
A joint between two parts placed end to end in the same plane.
A triangular weld joining two surfaces at an angle, as in a lap or T-joint.
The part of the parent metal that melts during welding and solidifies with or without filler metal.
Oxy-acetylene flame with oxygen and acetylene near 1:1; about 3200 °C; used for steel welding.
Oxy-acetylene flame with excess oxygen; it is oxidising to steel and is used only where that effect is acceptable.
Oxy-acetylene flame with excess acetylene; it is reducing and lower in temperature than the neutral flame.
Curve of arc voltage against arc current at a fixed arc length; its slope decides whether a drooping, flat or rising source can hold the arc steady.
Power source with a steep drooping V-I curve; it holds current nearly fixed as arc length changes, as needed for SMAW and TIG.
Power source with a flat V-I curve; it holds voltage nearly fixed while current changes with wire feed or arc length, as used in MIG and SAW.
Electrode code: E = electrode; 60 = 60 ksi minimum tensile strength; 1 = all positions; 3 = rutile-type coating for AC or DC.
Electrode code: E = electrode; 70 = 70 ksi minimum tensile strength; 1 = all positions; 8 = low-hydrogen iron-powder coating, usually DC.
Joining by passing a large current through contacting sheets; heat I²Rt at the interface forms a molten nugget.
Solid-state joining with a rotating non-consumable tool that stirs plasticised metal; the metal does not melt.
MIG variant with a controlled short circuit and wire retraction; it gives low heat input and low spatter.
Gas pockets trapped in weld metal, caused by moisture, dirt, poor shielding or wrong current.

takeaways: Every joining process is classified by what melts: the parent metal in fusion welding, nothing in solid-state welding, or only a lower-melting filler in brazing and soldering.
An oxy-acetylene flame is set by the oxygen-to-acetylene ratio; the neutral flame is the normal choice for steel.
The welding arc is a conducting gas, and its voltage-current curve decides which power source can hold it steady.
SMAW, TIG, MIG and SAW differ mainly in how they shield molten metal from air and how they add filler.
Resistance spot welding makes heat inside the joint at the contact resistance between sheets, so the nugget forms where the surfaces touch.
Solid-state welding joins by pressure, heat and diffusion without melting, which suits dissimilar metals and low-distortion work.
Laser welding and cold metal transfer reduce heat input and distortion for thin or dissimilar parts.
Brazing, soldering and adhesive bonding leave the parent metal unmelted and allow dissimilar materials to be joined.
Most weld defects come from poor control of heat, cleanliness and air protection; each defect has a suitable inspection method.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress classification, process sketches, arc and power-source characteristics, process comparisons, defect causes and remedies, and the distinction between brazing and soldering.

bank.q: Explain the physics of the welding arc and its voltage-current characteristic. Compare constant current and constant voltage power sources and state where each is used.

Contact resistance and bulk resistance

bank.q: Explain friction welding, friction stir welding, ultrasonic welding, explosive welding and diffusion bonding as solid-state joining processes.
outline: Solid-state joining: clean surfaces, pressure, heat, diffusion
Friction welding: relative motion, friction heat, axial force
Friction stir welding: rotating tool, plasticised metal, no melting
Ultrasonic welding: scrubbing action and pressure
Explosive welding: detonation, wavy interface, large area
Diffusion bonding: temperature, pressure, time in vacuum

bank.q: Describe laser welding and cold metal transfer welding. Explain how each limits heat input and distortion, and give suitable applications.
outline: Laser: high power density, small spot, conduction or keyhole mode
Keyhole gives deep narrow penetration
CMT: controlled short circuit with wire retraction
Low heat input, low spatter, thin sheets
Dissimilar and coated materials
Automobile and precision joining

bank.q: Explain brazing, soldering and adhesive bonding. Include filler melting ranges, flux action, capillary flow and joint design.

Soldering: filler below 450 °C
Flux removes oxide and improves wetting
Capillary action and joint clearance

bank.q: Identify common welding defects such as porosity, slag inclusion, lack of fusion, undercut, cracking and distortion. Explain their causes, remedies and inspection methods.
outline: Defect causes: heat, dirt, moisture, poor shielding
Porosity and slag inclusion

bank.q: A car body needs thin aluminium sheets joined with low distortion and good appearance. Select a suitable process from TIG, MIG, laser, CMT, resistance spot and friction stir welding. Justify the choice and state two precautions.
outline: Thin aluminium: low heat input needed
CMT or laser or resistance spot suitable
TIG and MIG possible but distortion risk
Friction stir for solid-state aluminium joining

bank.q: A steel pressure vessel is to be welded from thick plates. Choose between SMAW, TIG, MIG and SAW, select a suitable electrode, and explain the power source and shielding method.
outline: Thick steel favours SAW for high deposition
SMAW for site or positional work
E7018 low-hydrogen electrode for cracking resistance
Constant current source for SMAW; constant voltage for SAW
Flux or gas shielding

bank.q: Using the arc characteristic, analyse why a constant current source holds a stable current when the welder changes arc length, while a constant voltage source holds a stable voltage. Explain the consequence for SMAW and MIG.
outline: Arc voltage rises with arc length at fixed current
Drooping source: small current change for large voltage change
Flat source: large current change for small voltage change
SMAW manual arc length variation: constant current suits
MIG wire feed and arc length self-regulation: constant voltage suits
Burn-off rate and stability

bank.q: A welded joint shows porosity and lack of fusion. Trace the likely causes back to heat control, cleanliness and air protection. Propose remedies and choose inspection methods to confirm the repair.
outline: Porosity: moisture, dirt, poor shielding, wrong current
Lack of fusion: low heat input, wrong angle, fast travel, oxide
Heat control: current, voltage, travel speed
Cleanliness: degreasing, wire brushing, dry electrodes
Shielding: gas flow, flux, wind protection
Inspection: visual, penetrant, ultrasonic, radiography; repair and retest

bank.q: Compare fusion welding with solid-state welding for joining copper to aluminium. Discuss heat, intermetallic formation, distortion, defects and likely service performance.
outline: Fusion welding: melting, brittle intermetallics, porosity, distortion
Solid-state: friction, ultrasonic, explosive or diffusion bonding
Lower heat and limited intermetallic growth
Surface cleaning and oxide removal
Joint strength and electrical conductivity
Inspection and applications

glossary.def: A joining process that produces coalescence of materials by heating, pressure or both, with or without filler.
Welding in which the parent metal melts at the joint and solidifies to form the weld.
Welding in which the parent metal remains solid and coalescence occurs by pressure, heat and diffusion.
Joining with a filler metal that melts above 450 °C but below the parent metal and flows by capillary action.
Joining with a filler metal that melts below 450 °C and wets the parent surfaces without melting them.
Joining two surfaces with a non-metallic adhesive that sets by chemical reaction, solvent loss or cooling.
A fusion weld made without added filler metal.
The formation of one continuous body from two contacting surfaces by atomic or molecular attraction.
A joint between two members placed end to end.
A joint in which one member overlaps another and is welded at the edge.
A joint in which one member meets another at approximately 90° to form a T shape.
A triangular weld placed in the corner between two surfaces at an angle.
The region of parent metal that melts during welding and solidifies as part of the weld.
The parent metal near the weld that does not melt but whose properties change because of the heat.
An oxy-acetylene flame with oxygen and acetylene near a 1:1 ratio.
An oxy-acetylene flame with excess acetylene, giving a reducing atmosphere.
An oxy-acetylene flame with excess oxygen, giving an oxidising atmosphere.
A sustained electrical discharge through ionised gas that produces heat between an electrode and the work.
The percentage of a 10-minute period for which a power source can carry its rated current without overheating.
A resistance welding process that makes a local molten nugget between overlapping sheets held under electrode force.
A solid-state process in which a rotating tool stirs plasticised metal along a seam without melting it.
A controlled MIG process with short-circuit transfer and wire retraction, giving low heat input.
A weld defect consisting of gas pockets trapped in the solidified weld metal.
A weld defect in which the weld metal fails to fuse to the parent metal or to a previous pass.
A surface inspection method in which a liquid dye enters surface-breaking defects and is then revealed.
Internal inspection using X-rays or gamma rays, where density differences show defects on a detector.
